items.new: It was not very long after speaking the Goney that another homeward-bound whaleman, the Town-Ho,* was encountered. She was manned almost entirely by Polynesians. In the short gam that followed, she gave us strong news of Moby Dick. For some of us, the general interest in the White Whale was now wildly heightened by a circumstance of the Town-Ho's story, which seemed obscurely to involve the whale in a certain wondrous, inverted visitation of one of those so-called judgments of God that are sometimes said to overtake certain men. This circumstance, with its own particular accompaniments, forming what may be called the secret part of the tragedy about to be told, never reached the ears of Captain Ahab or his mates. For that secret part of the story was unknown even to the captain of the Town-Ho himself. It was the private property of three white seamen of that ship who were in league together, one of whom, it seems, passed it on to Tashtego under Romish injunctions of secrecy; but the following night Tashtego rambled in his sleep, and revealed so much of it that way that, when he was woken, he could not well hold back the rest. Nevertheless, so powerful an influence did this thing have on those seamen in the Pequod who came to know it fully, and by such a strange delicacy, so to call it, were they governed in this matter, that they kept the secret among themselves, so that it never traveled aft of the Pequod's mainmast. Weaving this darker thread into its proper place in the story as publicly told on the ship, I now set the whole of this strange affair down on lasting record.

items.new: "Some two years before I first learned of the events I am about to recount to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the north of the Line. One morning, when the pumps were worked, as was the daily custom, it was noticed that she was taking more water into her hold than usual. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain had some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and was therefore very unwilling to leave them; and since the leak was not then considered at all dangerous (though, in fact, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather), the ship went on with her cruising, the sailors working at the pumps at long and easy intervals. But no good luck came. More days went by, and not only was the leak still undiscovered, but it noticeably increased. So much so that the captain, now taking some alarm, made all sail and headed for the nearest harbor among the islands, to have his hull hove out and repaired there."

items.new: "Though no short passage lay ahead of her, yet if the commonest luck held, he did not at all fear that his ship would founder on the way, because his pumps were of the best, and, taking turns at them, his thirty-six men could easily keep the ship free of water, never mind if the leak should double. In truth, since nearly the whole of this passage was attended by very favorable breezes, the Town-Ho would all but certainly have reached her port in perfect safety, without the least fatality, had it not been for the brutal overbearing of Radney, the mate, a Vineyarder from Martha's Vineyard, and the bitterly provoked vengeance of Steelkilt, a Lakeman and desperado from Buffalo."

items.new: "On the eastern shore of our Lake Erie, Don; but — I beg your patience — perhaps you shall soon hear more of all that. Now, gentlemen, in square-sail brigs and three-masted ships, nearly as large and sturdy as any that ever sailed out of your old Callao to far Manila, this Lakeman, in the landlocked heart of our America, had nonetheless been raised on all those agrarian, freebooting impressions popularly connected with the open ocean. For taken all together, those grand freshwater seas of ours — Erie, and Ontario, and Huron, and Superior, and Michigan — have an ocean-like expanse, with many of the ocean's noblest traits, and with many of its varieties of races and climates around their rims. They contain round archipelagoes of romantic islands, just as the Polynesian waters do; for much of their length they are bordered by two great contrasting nations, as the Atlantic is; they provide long sea approaches to our many territorial colonies from the East, dotted all around their banks; here and there they are frowned upon by batteries, and by the goat-like, craggy guns of lofty Mackinaw; they have heard the swift thunder of naval victories; at intervals they yield their beaches to wild barbarians, whose red-painted faces flash out from their fur-hide wigwams; for leagues and leagues they are flanked by ancient, untrodden forests, where the gaunt pines stand like serried lines of kings in Gothic family trees, those same woods sheltering wild African beasts of prey, and silky-coated creatures whose exported furs make robes for Tartar Emperors; they mirror the paved capitals of Buffalo and Cleveland, as well as Winnebago villages; they float alike the full-rigged merchant ship, the armed cruiser of the State, the steamer, and the beech canoe; they are swept by north winds and dismasting blasts as terrible as any that lash the salt sea; they know what shipwrecks are, for out of sight of land, however inland, they have drowned many a ship at midnight with all its shrieking crew. So, gentlemen, though an inlander, Steelkilt was born to the wild ocean and raised on the wild ocean — as bold a mariner as any. And as for Radney: though as an infant he may have lain down on the lonely Nantucket beach to nurse at his mother the sea; though in later life he had long followed our austere Atlantic and your contemplative Pacific — he was still quite as vengeful and quarrelsome as the backwoods seaman fresh from the latitudes of buckhorn-handled Bowie knives. Yet this Nantucketer was a man with some good-hearted traits; and this Lakeman was a mariner who, though a sort of devil indeed, could still be handled by unbending firmness, tempered only by that common decency of human recognition which is the right of the lowliest slave; treated that way, this Steelkilt had long been kept harmless and docile. At any rate, he had proved so up to then; but Radney was doomed and driven mad, and Steelkilt — but, gentlemen, you shall hear."

items.new: "It was not more than a day or two at most after she had pointed her bow toward her island harbor that the Town-Ho's leak seemed to be increasing again, though only enough to require an hour or more at the pumps every day. You must know that in a settled and civilized ocean like our Atlantic, for example, some captains think little of pumping their whole way across it — though on a still, sleepy night, should the officer of the deck happen to forget his duty in that respect, the likelihood is that he and his shipmates would never remember it again, because all hands would be gently settling to the bottom. Nor in the lonely and savage seas far to the west of you, gentlemen, is it altogether unusual for ships to keep clanging at their pump-handles in full chorus even over a voyage of considerable length; that is, if it runs along a fairly accessible coast, or if some other reasonable refuge is open to them. It is only when a leaky vessel is in some very out-of-the-way part of those waters, some truly landless latitude, that her captain begins to feel a little anxious."

items.new: "Much this way it had been with the Town-Ho. So when her leak was found gaining once more, there was in truth some small concern shown by several of her company, especially by Radney the mate. He ordered the upper sails to be well hoisted, sheeted home anew, and every way spread to the breeze. Now this Radney, I suppose, was as little of a coward, and as little inclined to any sort of nervous fear for his own person, as any fearless, unthinking creature on land or on sea that you can conveniently imagine, gentlemen. So when he showed this anxiety about the safety of the ship, some of the seamen declared that it was only because he was a part owner in her. And so, when they were working at the pumps that evening, there was no small amount of sly joking going on among them on this point, as they stood with their feet continually washed over by the rippling clear water — clear as any mountain spring, gentlemen — that bubbled from the pumps, ran across the deck, and poured itself out in steady spouts at the lee scupper-holes."

items.new: Freely portrayed in his own calling, gentlemen, the Canaller would make a fine dramatic hero, so abundantly and picturesquely wicked is he. Like Mark Antony, for days and days along his green-turfed, flowery Nile, he lazily floats, openly toying with his red-cheeked Cleopatra, ripening his apricot thigh on the sunny deck. But ashore, all this softness is dashed away. The brigand-like getup the Canaller so proudly sports, and his slouched and gaily ribboned hat, proclaim his grand features. A terror to the smiling innocence of the villages he floats through, his swarthy face and bold swagger are shunned in the cities too. Once, when I was a vagabond on his own canal, I received good turns from one of these Canallers; I thank him heartily, and would not wish to be ungrateful; but it is often one of the chief redeeming qualities of your man of violence that at times he has as stiff an arm to back a poor stranger in a tight spot as to rob a wealthy one. In sum, gentlemen, how wild this canal life is, is emphatically shown by this: that our wild whale-fishery contains so many of its most finished graduates, and that hardly any breed of men, except Sydney men, are so much distrusted by our whaling captains. Nor does it at all lessen the curiousness of this matter that, for many thousands of our country boys and young men born along its route, the probationary life of the Grand Canal furnishes the only transition between quietly reaping in a Christian cornfield and recklessly plowing the waters of the most barbaric seas."

items.new: No need, gentlemen; one moment, and I'll go on. — Now, gentlemen, suddenly seeing the snowy whale within fifty yards of the ship — forgetting the pact among the crew — in the excitement of the moment the Teneriffe man had instinctively and involuntarily raised his voice for the monster, though for some little time past it had been plainly visible from the three sullen mastheads. Everything was now a frenzy. 'The White Whale — the White Whale!' was the cry from captain, mates, and harpooners, who, undeterred by fearful rumors, were all eager to capture so famous and precious a fish; while the sullen crew eyed sideways, and with curses, the appalling beauty of the vast milky mass that, lit up by the level, spangling rays of the sun, shifted and glistened like a living opal in the blue morning sea. Gentlemen, a strange fatality runs through the whole course of these events, as if truly mapped out before the world itself was charted. The mutineer was the mate's bowsman, and when they were fast to a whale, it was his duty to sit next to him, while Radney stood up with his lance in the bow, and to haul in or slacken the line at the word of command. Moreover, when the four boats were lowered, the mate's got the start; and no one howled more fiercely with delight than Steelkilt as he strained at his oar. After a hard pull, their harpooner got fast, and, spear in hand, Radney sprang to the bow. He was always a furious man in a boat, it seems. And now his bandaged cry was to beach him on the whale's topmost back. Only too willing, his bowsman hauled him up and up, through a blinding foam that blended two whitenesses together, until suddenly the boat struck as if against a sunken ledge, and, tipping over, spilled out the standing mate. At that instant, as he fell on the whale's slippery back, the boat righted and was dashed aside by the swell, while Radney was tossed over into the sea on the other flank of the whale. He struck out through the spray, and for an instant was dimly seen through that veil, wildly trying to get himself out of the eye of Moby Dick. But the whale rushed around in a sudden maelstrom, seized the swimmer between his jaws, and, rearing high up with him, plunged headlong again and went down."
